newsitem.title: INDIA: Daewoo, W.I. Carr analysts views on Indian markets.
newsitem.headline: Daewoo, W.I. Carr analysts views on Indian markets.

text.p: Following are the views of two analysts interviewed by Reuters Financial Television on Wednesday on how India's political crisis could affects its financial markets and the future course the markets could take:
Tushar Sarda, President and chief executive officer at Daewoo Securities in Bombay AND Dilip Rathore, senior economist at W.I. Carr in Singapore: --
Q. Foreign investors seem to have been caught unawares by those political developments over the weekend. Do you think the markets have over-reacted somewhat?
SARDA
"I think the markets over-reacted on Monday, but since yesterday they have started recovering and I expect the recovery to continue over next couple of days."
Q. What kind of specific levels are you looking at? Do you see support rather strong around the current level it holds?
SARDA

"I would expect all the losses to be recovered. On Monday, the market had fallen by about 300 points. I expect the entire losses to be recovered. The markets had gone down on the expectation that the government would be dismissed and the budget may not be passed in parliament.

But, what has emerged in the last couple of days is that there is a broad consensus amongst all political parties that it was a good budget and all efforts must be made to pass the budget. That should boost the confidence of foreign investors in India."
Q. Do you think that any other surprises are out there for investors or is most of the bad news out of the way and the focus will be on just passage of the budget?
RATHORE

"No, the focus will be on the passage of the budget, there is no doubt about it. But, I don't think all the bad news is out of the way yet. Because, we still don't know what the political outcome will be, which means there might be a delay in finally getting the economic management acts together finally.

It could take about three months or maybe even four months before they can really start implementing the reforms program... but I don't see any major threat to the new economic reforms program that were announced in the budget which was very pro-market and...I would say very good."
Q. What kind of investor strategy would you recommend towards India?
RATHORE

"I would recomend actually buying on the dip right now, because long term and medium term, India does offer very good earnings prospect... The growth in particular, GDP (Gross Domestic Product) is going to take off and people are now talking about an eight percent growth.
In that set-up, I would think investors should just set aside political considerations as long as they can hold onto their investments for maybe, a year.

Q. How would you describe the recent investor flow into India? Has it been investors with -- that kind of year outlook or more medium term outlook or has it been...people look for a quick market ride and to get out just as quickly?
SARDA

"I think the money which has come into India since 1992, initially it was short-term money, when investors were looking for a quick ride on the market. But, what has happened over the past 1-1/2 years is that we have seen money flowing into the country from investors who are really committed to India and who are investing over a longer time frame.

I would think that their time frame would be a minimum of five years. They would really not be disturbed by what has happened over the week-end. In fact on Monday and Tuesday, we saw very strong buying from these long-term committed investors."
Q. Again, the confidence vote coming up in the next few weeks, do you expect the market to bounce back significantly.
RATHORE

"Not in the next few weeks. I would think that the market would wait for a while. It all depends on how the political event shapes up during the course of this week itself. But, I do not expect any major improvement in the market. For example, coming back to the same level as the last week in the short-term."
Q. Staying with that, the currency has been rather untouched by the political situation. Do you think it could become vulnerable or do you think the central bank would dampen any speculation.?
RATHORE

"The central bank is going to intervene as they have intervened always in the past, and now of course, they are backed by huge foreign exchange reserves. Since you know, one of the reasons why imports of consumer goods were liberalised was because the rupee was under buying pressure, for a change...

But, even if there is an outflow of capital and there is selling of rupees. I think the Reserve Bank of India has enough reserves to defend it and they will intervene in the market. So, I would expect the rupee to remain stable against the US dollar.
Q. In terms of the size of the budge and its passage, what is key to further investment growth into India from here."
SARDA

"The crisis has given a message that there is a political consensus on the reforms and I think that would be the key to the further growth of investment into the country. Whether it is the Congress party or the United Front or the Bharatiya Janata Party, everybody is agreed that the reforms must continue.
And therefore, the political risks of investments into India comes down significantly.
The only worrying factor is that there should be some government which continues with announcement of policy measures and implementation of these things. We should not lose too much time on that."
RATHORE

I think.. economic reforms are the most important, guiding factor for foreign investors right now and if there is some chance of political stability, that should be positive for the foreign investment inflows...
I think all political parties are now agreed on the course of reform, that the economy has to become pro-market and they have to go for economic liberalisation. That is in the positive direction.

The only problem is in implementation of the policies for which political stability is important. And, we do need to see a stable government, otherwise we will continue to see some sort of fluctuation in the market mood.
The other important point..is that they have to do something about the infrastructure sector which is always causing some long term worries for investors.
